summary: This standards-track RFC specifies how SIP, SDP and RTP deliver real-time media and metadata from a communication session to a recording device. It sets up a Recording Session between a Session Recording Client on the call path and a Session Recording Server.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes how a device sitting in the middle of a phone call can send a copy of the call, and a running description of who was on it, to a recording server. It also defines how the people on the call can be told that a recording is taking place, and how they can say whether they mind.

questions: how does sip call recording work
what is the sdp record attribute
subtitle: How a call-path device streams a copy of a live call, plus notes about it, to a recording server using SIP, SDP and RTP.

tldr.problem: A call recording system needs a copy of the call's media and a description of who was in it, and there was no standard way for a device sitting on the call path to set that up with a recording server.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Recording Session between a Session Recording Client on the call path and a Session Recording Server at the recording device, using SIP to set it up, SDP to describe the recorded streams, and RTP to carry them, together with a metadata format and SDP attributes for recording indication and preference.
tldr.outcome: The result is that any device on the call path can stream a copy of a live call to a recorder and describe it, and the participants can be told that recording is taking place. RFC 7866 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 9806.

today: RFC 7866 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 9806. It has not been obsoleted, so the recording session it defines is the one to implement.

sections.title: What the Session Recording Protocol Does
sections.content:
This document specifies the mechanism to record a Communication Session (CS) by delivering real-time media and metadata from the CS to a recording device. In accordance with the architecture of RFC 7245, the Session Recording Protocol specifies the use of SIP, the Session Description Protocol (SDP) and RTP to establish a Recording Session (RS) between the Session Recording Client (SRC), which is on the path of the CS, and the Session Recording Server (SRS) at the recording device. SIP is also used to deliver metadata to the recording device, as specified in RFC 7865. Metadata is information that describes recorded media and the CS to which they relate.

The protocol is meant to satisfy the SIP-based Media Recording (SIPREC) requirements listed in RFC 6341. In addition to the Session Recording Protocol itself, the document specifies extensions for user agents that are participants in a CS, so that they can receive recording indications and provide preferences for recording.

Only active recording is considered here, where the SRC purposefully streams media to an SRS and all participating user agents are notified of the recording. Passive recording, where a recording device detects media directly from the network, for example using port-mirroring techniques, is outside the scope of this document, and so is lawful intercept.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC describes how a device in the middle of a phone call can send a copy of the call, and a description of who was on it, to a recording server. It also defines how the people on the call can be told that a recording is taking place.

sections.title: What Is Out of Scope
sections.content:
The scope includes the establishment of the recording sessions and the reporting of the metadata. It also includes extensions supported by user agents participating in the communication session, such as an indication of recording. The user agents do not need to be recording aware in order to take part in a call that is being recorded.

Several things are explicitly outside the protocol and are listed as out of scope: delivering recorded media in real time as the call media; specifications of criteria to select a specific call to be recorded, or triggers to record a call in the future; recording policies that determine whether a call should be recorded and whether parts of it are to be recorded; retention policies that determine how long a recording is stored; searching and accessing the recorded media and metadata; policies governing how call users are made aware of recording; and delivering additional recording metadata through a non-SIP mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC is about setting up the recording and describing it. Deciding what to record, how long to keep it and who may listen to it are somebody else's job.

sections.title: How a Recording Is Made
sections.content:
There are a number of call flows depending on where the SRC sits. When a SIP Back-to-Back User Agent (B2BUA) with SRC functionality routes a call from UA A to UA B, the SRC has access to the media path between them. When the SRC is aware that it should be recording the conversation, it can cause the B2BUA to relay the media between UA A and UA B, and then establish the recording session with the SRS and send replicated media towards the SRS. An endpoint may also have SRC functionality, where the endpoint itself establishes the recording session and sends replicated media towards the SRS.

Figure 1 shows a UA acting as the SRC. The call is set up with a CS INVITE and a 200 OK. The SRC then sends an RS INVITE with SDP to the SRS, which answers with a 200 OK with SDP. The media of the call flows between the two users, and a copy of it flows from the SRC to the SRS. When the call ends, a CS BYE and an RS BYE are exchanged. The SRC can choose when to establish the recording session independently of the call, even though the example flows show it being established after the call.

The same flow applies when a B2BUA acts as the SRC, and it also applies to a centralized conference with a mixer: the conference focus can provide the SRC functionality, because it has access to all the media from each participant. When a recording is requested, the SRC delivers the metadata and the media streams to the SRS, and it may choose to mix the media streams from all participants into a single mixed stream. An SRC can also use a single recording session to record multiple calls, updating the session with a new SDP offer to add new recorded streams and correspondingly updating the metadata for the new call.

Metadata is delivered by the SRC. It may provide an initial metadata snapshot in the initial INVITE content of the recording session, and subsequent metadata updates can be represented as a stream of events in UPDATE or re-INVITE requests. Those updates are normally incremental updates to the initial snapshot, which keeps the messages small, but the SRC may also decide to send a new snapshot at any time. The SRS has the ability to ask the SRC for a new snapshot, which can happen when the SRS fails to understand the current stream of incremental updates, for example when it loses the current state due to internal failure. That request lets both sides synchronise their state so that further incremental updates are based on the latest snapshot.
sections.plainLanguage: The device on the call path opens a second, separate conversation with the recorder. It copies the call's audio and video into that conversation, and it sends a running description of who is speaking.

sections.title: Setting Up the Recording Session
sections.content:
A recording session is a SIP session with specific extensions applied. The SRC can initiate one by sending a SIP INVITE request to the SRS, with the SRC and the SRS identified in the From and To headers respectively. The SRC MUST include the "+sip.src" feature tag in the Contact URI, defined as an extension to RFC 3840, for all recording sessions. The SRS uses the presence of that tag in dialog creating and modifying requests and responses to confirm that the dialog is for the purpose of a recording session. When an SRC sends a REGISTER request to a registrar it MAY include the same tag to indicate that it is an SRC.

Because SIP Caller Preferences extensions are optional to implement for routing proxies, there is no guarantee that a recording session will be routed to an SRC or an SRS. A new option tag, "siprec", is introduced for that reason. Only an SRC or an SRS can accept this option tag in a recording session, and the SRC MUST include it in the Require header when initiating a recording session, so that user agents which do not support the Session Recording Protocol extensions simply reject the INVITE request with a 420 (Bad Extension) response.

When an SRC receives a new INVITE it MUST only consider the SIP session to be a recording session when both the "+sip.srs" feature tag and the "siprec" option tag are included in the request. The SRS follows the mirror image. It can initiate a recording session by sending an INVITE to the SRC; it MUST include the "+sip.srs" feature tag in the Contact URI for all recording sessions; and it SHOULD include that tag when it sends a REGISTER request. An SRS MUST include the "siprec" option tag in the Require header when it initiates a recording session.

For the participants in the call, a recording-aware UA indicates that it can accept recording indications with a new "record-aware" option tag, included in the Supported header in the initial INVITE request or response. A recording-aware UA MUST then provide a recording indication to the end user through an appropriate user interface, indicating whether recording is on, off or paused for each medium. User agents that are automatons, such as an Interactive Voice Response system, a media server or a PSTN gateway, may have no user interface to render a recording indication. When such a UA indicates recording awareness, it SHOULD render the indication through other means, such as an in-band tone on the gateway, a log file or an application event in a VoiceXML dialog. These UAs MAY also choose not to indicate recording awareness at all, relying on whatever mechanism the SRC chooses to use.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends mark the conversation so that proxies can route it and so that anything else knows to stay out. The participants who want to know about recording say so up front, and are then told whether recording is on.

sections.title: Describing the Media: SDP and Its Attributes
sections.content:
The SRC and SRS follow the SDP offer/answer model described in RFC 3264. Because the SRC does not expect to receive media from the SRS, the SRC typically sets each media stream of its SDP offer to only send media, by qualifying it with the "a=sendonly" attribute. The SRC sends recorded streams of participants to the SRS and MUST provide a "label" attribute, "a=label", on each media stream in order to identify the recorded stream with the rest of the metadata. The label name is mapped to the Media Stream Reference in the metadata. The scope of the attribute applies only to the SDP and metadata conveyed in the body of the SIP request or response in which it appeared. A recorded stream is distinct from a call stream, because the metadata provides a list of the participants that contribute to each recorded stream.

Over the lifetime of a recording session the SRC can add and remove recorded streams, for example when a call stream is added to or removed from the call, or when a call is created or terminated in a session that handles several calls. To remove a recorded stream the SRC sends a new SDP offer where the port of that media stream is set to zero. To add one it sends a new SDP offer with a new media stream description, or reuses a previously disabled media stream. The SRC can also temporarily stop streaming and collecting recorded media, for example to mask the recording, by sending a new SDP offer that sets the media stream to inactive with "a=inactive", and resumes by setting it back to "a=sendonly". A call may itself change the direction of a media stream, for example by setting inactive for hold; those changes are conveyed in the metadata by the SRC, and the effect on the corresponding recording session stream is governed by SRC policy.

Two new SDP attributes carry the recording state. The "record" attribute appears at the media level or the session level in an SDP offer or answer. Applied at the session level, the indication applies to all media streams in the SDP; applied at the media level, it applies to that one media stream and overrides a session-level indication. Whenever the recording indication needs to change, such as at termination of recording, the SRC MUST initiate a re-INVITE or UPDATE to update the attribute. Its allowed values are on, meaning that recording is in progress, off, meaning that no recording is in progress, and paused, meaning that recording is in progress but the media is paused.

The "recordpref" attribute is the counterpart sent by the participant. When the SRC receives it in an SDP offer or answer, the SRC chooses whether to honour the preference to record based on local policy at the SRC. If the SRC makes a change in recording state, it MUST report the new state in the "a=record" attribute in the SDP answer or in a subsequent SDP offer. The allowed values are on, off, pause and nopreference.

The SRS, which typically only receives RTP streams from the SRC, normally sets each media stream in its answer to receive media with the "a=recvonly" attribute. When the SRS is not ready to receive a recorded stream it sets the stream inactive with "a=inactive", and when it is ready it sends a new SDP offer with the streams set to "a=recvonly". The SRS MUST NOT add recorded streams when it sends a new SDP offer, and when the SRS starts a recording session it MUST initiate the INVITE without an SDP offer, to let the SRC generate the offer with the streams to be recorded.
sections.plainLanguage: Each recorded stream gets a name in the session description, so that the description of the call can point at it. Two new attributes say whether recording is on, and what the participant would prefer.

sections.title: Carrying the Media: RTP and the SRC's Roles
sections.content:
Section 8 gives recommendations and guidelines for RTP and RTCP in the context of SIPREC. The RTP data transport is augmented by a control protocol, RTCP, which is based on the periodic transmission of control packets to all participants in the RTP session using the same distribution mechanism as the data packets. Support for RTCP is required, and it provides two things that matter here. The first is feedback on the quality of the data distribution, so that the SRS can inform the SRC, and the SRC can inform recording-aware user agents, about problems with the reception of media that is to be recorded. The second is a persistent transport-level identifier, the CNAME, for an RTP source: the synchronization source identifier may change if a conflict is discovered or a program is restarted, in which case receivers can use the CNAME to keep track of each participant and to associate multiple data streams from one participant, for example to synchronise audio and video.

The recommended RTP profiles are RTP/SAVPF when using encrypted RTP streams and RTP/AVPF when using non-encrypted ones. Because these are recommendations rather than requirements, some implementations use SRTP and the RTP profile for audio and video conferences with minimal control instead. The RFC therefore recommends that the SRC, SRS and recording-aware user agents do not rely entirely on the feedback profiles for core functionality. SAVP and SAVPF provide media encryption, integrity protection, replay protection and a limited form of source authentication, and they do not contain or require a specific keying mechanism.

The SRC gathers media from the various user agents in one or more communication sessions and forwards it to the SRS within the recording session. It may appear as a user agent within a call, or as a B2BUA between user agents, and because the call and the recording session are independent sessions, it may play a different role in the call than in the recording session. Three roles are defined. As an RTP translator, it forwards RTP packets with their SSRC identifier intact, so streams received separately from different sources cannot be mixed and must be sent separately to the SRS, and all RTCP reports must be passed between the user agents and the SRS so that both can detect SSRC collisions; a translator may also transcode. As an RTP mixer, it combines RTP streams from different user agents and sends them towards the SRS using its own SSRC, conveying the contributing SSRCs as CSRC identifiers, and it generates its own RTCP Sender and Receiver Reports. As an RTP endpoint, the RTP session between the SRC and the SRS is considered completely independent from the RTP session that is part of the call, and RTCP between the SRC and the SRS is completely independent of RTCP on the call.

For base interoperability between SRC and SRS, an SRC MUST support separate m-lines in SDP, one per call media direction. When sending RTP the use of symmetric RTP is required, and the same applies to symmetric RTCP.
sections.plainLanguage: The media itself is ordinary RTP. The extra parts are a control channel that reports quality problems, and a stable name for each participant so that the recorder can keep track of who is who even when a stream restarts.

sections.title: Metadata
sections.content:
Some metadata attributes are contained in SDP and others are contained in a new content type called "application/rs-metadata". The format of the metadata is described as part of the mechanism in RFC 7865. A new "disposition-type" of Content-Disposition is defined for the purpose of carrying metadata, with the value "recording-session", which indicates that the "application/rs-metadata" content contains metadata to be handled by the SRS.

The SRC MUST send metadata to the SRS in a recording session and SHOULD send it as soon as it becomes available and whenever it changes. There are cases in which an SRC may be justified in waiting temporarily: waiting for a previous metadata exchange to complete, constraining the signalling rate on the recording session, or sending metadata when key events occur rather than for every event that has any impact on metadata. The SRC may also be configured to suppress certain metadata out of concern for privacy, or for a perceived lack of need for it to be included in the recording.

Metadata sent by the SRC is either a full snapshot, which describes all the metadata associated with the recording session, or a partial update. The SRC MAY send a full snapshot at any time, and MAY send a partial update only if a full snapshot has been sent previously. Metadata may be sent in an INVITE request, an UPDATE request, or a 200 response to an offerless INVITE from the SRS, and if the metadata contains a reference to any SDP labels the request containing it MUST also contain an SDP offer that defines those labels. When a SIP message contains both an SDP offer and metadata, the request body MUST have the content type "multipart/mixed", with one subordinate body part containing the SDP offer and another containing the metadata. The SRC SHOULD include a full metadata snapshot in the initial INVITE request establishing the recording session, and if metadata is not yet available it SHOULD send a full snapshot as soon as it becomes available. If the SRC receives a snapshot request from the SRS, it MUST immediately send a full metadata snapshot.
sections.plainLanguage: The description of the call comes in two forms: a complete picture sent occasionally, and small changes in between. The recorder can always ask for a fresh complete picture if it has lost track.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The recording session is fundamentally a standard SIP dialog, so it can reuse any of the existing SIP security mechanisms available for securing the session signalling, the recorded media and the metadata. The SRC and SRS MUST support SIP with Transport Layer Security (TLS) version 1.2, SHOULD follow the best practices for TLS as per RFC 7525, and MAY use Session Initiation Protocol Secure (SIPS) with TLS. The recording session MUST be at least as secure as the communication session. If the call uses SIPS for signalling and RTP/SAVP for media, then the recording session may not use SIP or plain RTP unless other equivalent security measures are in effect, because doing so would mean an effective security downgrade.

At the transport level the recording session uses TLS authentication to validate the authenticity of the SRC and the SRS. The SRC and SRS MUST implement TLS mutual authentication for establishing the recording session, although whether they choose to do so is a deployment decision. Where the SRS can be hosted in a different administrative domain, it is important to perform mutual authentication before transmitting any recorded media: the risk of not authenticating the SRS is that the recording may be sent to an entity other than the intended one, allowing a sensitive call recording to be received by an attacker, and the risk of not authenticating the SRC is that the SRS will accept calls from an unknown SRC and allow potential forgery of call recordings.

For the media, the SRC and the SRS MUST support RTP/SAVP and RTP/SAVPF, and at a minimum the SDP security descriptions key negotiation mechanism. If an SRC simply replicates RTP packets from a call media stream to the SRS using the same key, it MUST secure the SDP containing the keying material in the recording session with at least the same level of security as in the call, because lowering it would effectively become a downgrade attack on the call. An SRC that decrypts an encrypted call media stream and re-encrypts it when sending it to the SRS MUST use a different key from the one used for the call, so that someone who holds the call key cannot access recorded data they are not authorised to access.

Metadata contains sensitive information, such as the addresses of participants, so it SHOULD be protected at the transport level by SIPS/TLS. Storage and playback of the recording are beyond the scope of the document, but the RFC notes that it is just as important: it would defeat the purpose of securing both the call and the recording session if the recording could be played back through a simple, unsecured HTTP interface with no form of authentication or authorization.
sections.plainLanguage: The recording session has to be at least as well protected as the call itself, and the two ends must check each other's identity before any audio or video is sent.

data.title: The record SDP attribute
data.code:
attribute =/ record-attr
; attribute defined in RFC 4566

record-attr = "record:" indication
indication = "on" / "off" / "paused"
